{{short description|Set of hyperedges where every pair is disjoint}}
[[File:Hypergraph matchings.svg|thumb|250px|The red set of edges is a '''perfect matching''', because it contains every vertex of the hypergraph. The yellow set is a '''maximum-cardinality matching''', because it contains the most edges possible for a matching in this hypergraph, and the '''matching number''' is therefore 3.

In a regular graph, if one has a perfect matching, that same matching is definitionally the maximum-cardinality matching for the graph, but in a hypergraph, where the number of vertices connected by an edge is variable, they can be 2 distinct matchings, as shown here.]]

In [[graph theory]], a '''matching''' in a [[hypergraph]] is a set of [[hyperedges]], in which every two hyperedges are [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]]. It is an extension of the notion of [[Matching (graph theory)|matching in a graph]].<ref name="lp">{{Cite Lovasz Plummer}}</ref>{{rp|466–470}} <ref>{{Cite book|last=Berge|first=Claude|title=Graphs and Hypergraphs|publisher=North-Holland|year=1973|location=Amsterdam}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Recall that a [[hypergraph]] {{mvar|H}} is a pair {{math|(''V'', ''E'')}}, where {{mvar|V}} is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] and {{mvar|E}} is a set of [[subset]]s of {{mvar|V}} called ''hyperedges''. Each hyperedge may contain one or more vertices.

A '''matching''' in {{mvar|H}} is a subset {{mvar|M}} of {{mvar|E}}, such that  every two hyperedges {{math|''e''{{sub|1}}}} and {{math|''e''{{sub|2}}}} in {{mvar|M}} have an empty intersection (have no vertex in common).

The '''matching number''' of a hypergraph {{mvar|H}} is the largest size of a matching in {{mvar|H}}. It is often denoted by {{math|ν(''H'')}}.<ref name="lp" />{{rp|466}} <ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Aharoni|first1=Ron|last2=Kessler|first2=Ofra|date=1990-10-15|title=On a possible extension of Hall's theorem to bipartite hypergraphs|journal=Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=84|issue=3|pages=309–313|doi=10.1016/0012-365X(90)90136-6|issn=0012-365X|doi-access=free}}</ref>

As an example, let {{mvar|V}} be the set {{math|{1,2,3,4,5,6,7}.}} Consider a 3-uniform hypergraph on {{mvar|V}} (a hypergraph in which each hyperedge contains exactly 3 vertices). Let {{mvar|H}} be a 3-uniform hypergraph with 4 hyperedges:

: {{math|{ {1,2,3}, {1,4,5}, {4,5,6}, {2,3,6} } }}

Then {{mvar|H}} admits several matchings of size 2, for example:

: {{math|{ {1,2,3}, {4,5,6} } }}
: {{math|{ {1,4,5}, {2,3,6} } }}
However, in any subset of 3 hyperedges, at least two of them intersect, so there is no matching of size 3. Hence, the matching number of {{mvar|H}} is 2.

== Intersecting hypergraph{{Anchor|intersecting}} ==
A hypergraph {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} is called ''intersecting'' if every two hyperedges in {{mvar|E}} have a vertex in common. A hypergraph {{mvar|H}} is intersecting [[if and only if]] it has no matching with two or more hyperedges, if and only if {{math|1=ν(''H'') = 1}}.<ref name=":2" />

== Matching in a graph as a special case ==
A graph without [[self-loop]]s is just a 2-uniform hypergraph: each edge can be considered as a set of the two vertices that it connects. For example, this 2-uniform hypergraph represents a graph with 4 vertices {{math|{1,2,3,4} }} and 3 edges:

: {{math|{ {1,3}, {1,4}, {2,4} } }}
By the above definition, a matching in a graph is a set {{mvar|M}} of edges, such that each two edges in {{mvar|M}} have an empty intersection. This is equivalent to saying that no two edges in {{mvar|M}} are adjacent to the same vertex; this is exactly the definition of a [[Matching (graph theory)|matching in a graph]].

== Fractional matching ==
A '''[[fractional matching]]''' in a hypergraph is a function that assigns a fraction in {{math|[0,1]}} to each hyperedge, such that for every vertex {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}}, the sum of fractions of hyperedges containing {{mvar|v}} is at most 1. A matching is a special case of a fractional matching in which all fractions are either 0 or 1.  The ''size'' of a fractional matching is the sum of fractions of all hyperedges.

The '''fractional matching number''' of a hypergraph {{mvar|H}} is the largest size of a fractional matching in {{mvar|H}}. It is often denoted by {{math|''ν''*(''H'')}}.<ref name=":1" />

Since a matching is a special case of a fractional matching, for every hypergraph {{mvar|H}}: <blockquote>Matching-number({{mvar|H}})   ≤   fractional-matching-number({{mvar|H}})</blockquote>
Symbolically, this principle is written:
:<math>\nu(H) \leq \nu^*(H) </math>

In general, the fractional matching number may be larger than the matching number.  A theorem by [[Zoltán Füredi]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Füredi|first=Zoltán|date=1981-06-01|title=Maximum degree and fractional matchings in uniform hypergraphs|journal=Combinatorica|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=155–162|doi=10.1007/BF02579271|s2cid=10530732|issn=1439-6912}}</ref> provides upper bounds on the fractional-matching-{{nowrap|number({{mvar|H}}) / matching-}}number({{mvar|H}}) ratio:

* If each hyperedge in {{mvar|H}} contains at most {{mvar|r}} vertices, then

<math>\frac{\nu^*(H)}{ \nu (H)} \leq r-1+ \frac{1}{r}.</math>

In particular, in a simple graph:<ref>{{Cite book|last=Lovász|first=L.|chapter=Minimax theorems for hypergraphs |date=1974|editor-last=Berge|editor-first=Claude|editor2-last=Ray-Chaudhuri|editor2-first=Dijen|title=Hypergraph Seminar|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics|volume=411|language=en|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer|pages=111–126|doi=10.1007/BFb0066186|isbn=978-3-540-37803-7}}</ref>

<math>\frac{\nu^*(H)}{ \nu (H)} \leq \frac{3}{2}.</math>

* The inequality is sharp: Let {{mvar|H{{sub|r}}}} be the {{mvar|r}}-uniform [[finite projective plane]]. Then  {{math|1=''ν''(''H''{{sub|''r''}}) = 1}} since every two hyperedges intersect, and {{math|1=''ν''*(''H''{{sub|''r''}}) = ''r'' – 1 + {{sfrac|1|''r''}}}} by the fractional matching that assigns a weight of {{math|{{sfrac|1|''r''}}}} to each hyperedge (it is a matching since each vertex is contained in {{mvar|r}} hyperedges, and its size is {{math|''r'' – 1 + {{sfrac|1|''r''}}}} since there are {{math|''r''{{sup|2}} – ''r'' + 1}} hyperedges). Therefore the ratio is exactly {{math|''r'' – 1 + {{sfrac|1|''r''}}}}.
* If {{mvar|r}} is such that the {{mvar|r}}-uniform [[finite projective plane]] does not exist (for example, {{math|1=''r'' = 7}}), then a stronger inequality holds:

<math>\frac{\nu^*(H)}{\nu (H)} \leq r-1.</math>

* If {{mvar|H}} is {{mvar|r}}-partite (the vertices are partitioned into {{mvar|r}} parts and each hyperedge contains a vertex from each part), then:

<math>\frac{\nu^*(H)}{\nu (H)} \leq r-1.</math>

In particular, in a bipartite graph, {{math|1=''ν''*(''H'') = ''ν''(''H'')}}. This was proved by [[András Gyárfás]].<ref name=":2" />

* The inequality is sharp: Let {{mvar|H{{sub|r-}}}} be the [[truncated projective plane]] of order {{math|''r'' – 1}}. Then {{math|1=''ν''(''H''{{sub|''r''-}}) = 1}} since every two hyperedges intersect, and {{math|1=''ν''*(''H''{{sub|''r''-}}) = ''r'' – 1}} by the fractional matching that assigns a weight of {{math|{{sfrac|1|''r''}}}} to each hyperedge (there are {{math|''r''{{sup|2}} – ''r''}} hyperedges).

== Perfect matching ==
A matching {{mvar|M}} is called '''perfect''' if every vertex {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}} is contained in ''exactly'' one hyperedge of {{mvar|M}}. This is the natural extension of the notion of [[perfect matching]] in a graph.

A fractional matching {{mvar|M}} is called '''perfect''' if for every vertex {{mvar|v}} in {{mvar|V}}, the sum of fractions of hyperedges in {{mvar|M}} containing {{mvar|v}} is ''exactly'' 1.

Consider a hypergraph {{mvar|H}} in which each hyperedge contains at most {{mvar|n}} vertices. If {{mvar|H}} admits a perfect fractional matching, then its fractional matching number is at least {{math|{{frac|{{abs|''V''}} |''n''}}}}. If each hyperedge in {{mvar|H}} contains exactly {{mvar|n}} vertices, then its fractional matching number is at exactly {{math|{{frac|{{abs|''V''}} |''n''}}}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Nyman|first1=Kathryn|last2=Su|first2=Francis Edward|last3=Zerbib|first3=Shira|date=2020-01-02|title=Fair division with multiple pieces|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X1930561X|journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics|volume=283|pages=115–122|language=en|arxiv=1710.09477|doi=10.1016/j.dam.2019.12.018|s2cid=119602376|issn=0166-218X}}</ref> {{Rp|sec.2}} This is a generalization of the fact that, in a graph, the size of a perfect matching is {{math|{{frac|{{abs|''V''}} |2}}}}.

Given a set {{mvar|V}} of vertices, a collection {{mvar|E}} of subsets of {{mvar|V}} is called ''balanced'' if the hypergraph {{math|(''V'',''E'')}} admits a perfect fractional matching.

For example, if {{math|1=''V'' = {1,2,3,a,b,c} }} and {{math|1=''E'' = { {1,a}, {2,a}, {1,b}, {2,b}, {3,c} },}} then {{mvar|E}} is balanced, with the perfect fractional matching {{math|{ 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1 }.}}

There are various sufficient conditions for the existence of a perfect matching in a hypergraph:

* [[Hall-type theorems for hypergraphs]] - presents sufficient conditions analogous to [[Hall's marriage theorem]], based on sets of neighbors. 
* [[Perfect matching in high-degree hypergraphs]] - presents sufficient conditions analogous to [[Dirac's theorem on Hamiltonian cycles]], based on degree of vertices. 
* [[Peter Keevash|Keevash]] and Mycroft developed a geometric theory for hypergraph matching.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Keevash|first1=Peter|url=https://www.ams.org/memo/1098/|title=A geometric theory for hypergraph matching|last2=Mycroft|first2=Richard|date=2015-01-01|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-1-4704-0965-4|series=Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society|volume=233|language=en}}</ref>

== Balanced set-family ==
A [[Family of sets|set-family]] {{mvar|E}} over a ground set {{mvar|V}} is called ''balanced'' (with respect to {{mvar|V}}) if the hypergraph {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} admits a perfect fractional matching.<ref name=":0" /> {{Rp|sec.2}}

For example, consider the vertex set {{math|1=''V'' = {1,2,3,a,b,c} }} and the edge set {{math|1=''E'' = {1-a, 2-a, 1-b, 2-b, 3-c}.}} {{mvar|E}} is balanced, since there is a perfect fractional matching with weights {{math|{1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1}.}}

== Computing a maximum matching ==
The problem of finding a maximum-cardinality matching in a hypergraph, thus calculating <math>\nu(H)</math>, is NP-hard even for 3-uniform hypergraphs (see [[3-dimensional matching]]). This is in contrast to the case of simple (2-uniform) graphs in which computing a [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum-cardinality matching]] can be done in polynomial time.

== Matching and covering ==
A [[Vertex cover in hypergraphs|''vertex-cover in a hypergraph'']] {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} is a subset {{mvar|T}} of {{mvar|V}}, such that every hyperedge in {{mvar|E}} contains at least one vertex of {{mvar|T}} (it is also called a [[Transversal (combinatorics)|'''transversal''']] or a '''[[hitting set]]''', and is equivalent to a [[Set cover problem|set cover]]). It is a generalization of the notion of a [[vertex cover]] in a graph.

The '''vertex-cover number''' of a hypergraph {{mvar|H}} is the smallest size of a vertex cover in {{mvar|H}}. It is often denoted by {{math|''τ''(''H'')}},<ref name="lp" />{{rp|466}} for transversal.

A '''fractional vertex-cover''' is a function assigning a weight to each vertex in {{mvar|V}}, such that for every hyperedge {{mvar|e}} in {{mvar|E}}, the sum of fractions of vertices in {{mvar|e}} is at least 1. A vertex cover is a special case of a fractional vertex cover in which all weights are either 0 or 1. The ''size'' of a fractional vertex-cover is the sum of fractions of all vertices.

The '''fractional vertex-cover number''' of a hypergraph {{mvar|H}} is the smallest size of a fractional vertex-cover in {{mvar|H}}.  It is often denoted by {{math|''τ''*(''H'')}}.

Since a vertex-cover is a special case of a fractional vertex-cover, for every hypergraph {{mvar|H}}:
<blockquote>fractional-vertex-cover-number ({{mvar|H}})  ≤   vertex-cover-number ({{mvar|H}}). </blockquote>
[[Linear programming duality]] implies that, for every hypergraph {{mvar|H}}:
<blockquote>fractional-matching-number ({{mvar|H}})  =  fractional-vertex-cover-number({{mvar|H}}). </blockquote>
Hence, for every hypergraph {{mvar|H}}:<ref name=":2" />
:<math>\nu(H) \leq \nu^*(H) =  \tau^*(H)\leq  \tau(H) </math>
If the size of each hyperedge in {{mvar|H}} is at most {{mvar|r}} then the union of all hyperedges in a maximum matching is a vertex-cover (if there was an uncovered hyperedge, we could have added it to the matching). Therefore:
:<math>\tau(H)\leq r\cdot \nu(H).</math>
This inequality is tight: equality holds, for example, when {{mvar|V}}  contains  {{math|''r''⋅''ν''(''H'') + ''r'' – 1}} vertices and {{mvar|E}} contains all subsets of {{mvar|r}} vertices.

However, in general {{math|''τ''*(''H'') <  ''r''⋅''ν''(''H'')}}, since {{math|''ν''*(''H'') < ''r''⋅''ν''(''H'')}}; see [[#Fractional matching|Fractional matching]] above.

''[[Ryser's conjecture]]'' says that, in every {{mvar|r}}-partite {{mvar|r}}-uniform hypergraph:
:<math>\tau (H)\leq (r-1) \nu(H).</math>
Some special cases of the conjecture have been proved; see [[Ryser's conjecture]].

== Kőnig's property ==
A hypergraph has the '''Kőnig property''' if its maximum matching number equals its minimum vertex-cover number, namely if {{math|1=''ν''(''H'') = ''τ''(''H'')}}. The [[Kőnig's theorem (graph theory)|Kőnig-Egerváry theorem]] shows that every [[bipartite graph]] has the Kőnig property. To extend this theorem to hypergraphs, we need to extend the notion of bipartiteness to hypergraphs.<ref name="lp" />{{rp|468}}

A natural generalization is as follows. A hypergraph is called '''2-colorable''' if its vertices can be 2-colored so that every hyperedge (of size at least 2) contains at least one vertex of each color. An alternative term is [[Property B]]. A simple graph is bipartite iff it is 2-colorable. However, there are 2-colorable hypergraphs without Kőnig's property. For example, consider the hypergraph with {{math|1=''V'' = {1,2,3,4} }} with all triplets {{math|1=''E'' = { {1,2,3} , {1,2,4} , {1,3,4} , {2,3,4} }.}} It is 2-colorable, for example, we can color {{math|{1,2} }} blue and {{math|{3,4} }} white. However, its matching number is 1 and its vertex-cover number is 2.

A stronger generalization is as follows. Given a hypergraph {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} and a subset {{mvar|V'}} of {{mvar|V}}, the '''restriction''' of {{mvar|H}} to {{mvar|V'}} is the hypergraph whose vertices are {{mvar|V}}, and for every hyperedge {{mvar|e}} in {{mvar|E}} that intersects {{mvar|V'}}, it has a hyperedge {{mvar|e'}} that is the intersection of {{mvar|e}} and {{mvar|V'}}. A hypergraph is called '''[[balanced hypergraph|balanced]]''' if all its restrictions are ''essentially 2-colorable'', meaning that we ignore singleton hyperedges in the restriction.<ref>{{Citation|last=Berge|first=CLAUDE|chapter=CHAPTER 2 – Balanced Hypergraphs and Some Applications to Graph Theory|date=1973-01-01|chapter-url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780720422627500077|title=A Survey of Combinatorial Theory|pages=15–23|editor-last=Srivastava|editor-first=JAGDISH N.|publisher=North-Holland|language=en|isbn=978-0-7204-2262-7|access-date=2020-06-19}}</ref> A simple graph is bipartite iff it is balanced.

A simple graph is bipartite iff it has no odd-length cycles. Similarly, a hypergraph is balanced iff it has no odd-length ''circuits''. A circuit of length {{mvar|k}} in a hypergraph is an alternating sequence {{math|1=(''v''{{sub|1}}, ''e''{{sub|1}}, ''v''{{sub|2}}, ''e''{{sub|2}}, …, ''v{{sub|k}}'', ''e{{sub|k}}'', ''v{{sub|k}}''{{sub|+1}} = ''v''{{sub|1}})}}, where the {{mvar|v{{sub|i}}}} are distinct vertices and the {{mvar|e{{sub|i}}}} are distinct hyperedges, and each hyperedge contains the vertex to its left and the vertex to its right. The circuit is called ''unbalanced'' if each hyperedge contains no other vertices in the circuit. [[Claude Berge]] proved that a hypergraph is balanced if and only if it does not contain an unbalanced odd-length circuit. Every balanced hypergraph has Kőnig's property.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Berge|first1=Claude|last2=Vergnas|first2=Michel LAS|date=1970|title=Sur Un Theorems Du Type König Pour Hypergraphes|journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=175|issue=1|pages=32–40|doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1970.tb56451.x|bibcode=1970NYASA.175...32B |s2cid=84670737 |issn=1749-6632}}</ref><ref name="lp" />{{Rp|468–470}}

The following are equivalent:<ref name="lp" />{{Rp|470–471}}

* Every partial hypergraph of {{mvar|H}} (i.e., a hypergraph derived from {{mvar|H}} by deleting some hyperedges) has the Kőnig property.
* Every partial hypergraph of {{mvar|H}} has the property that its maximum degree equals its minimum [[edge coloring]] number.
* {{mvar|H}} has the [[Helly property]], and the [[intersection graph]] of {{mvar|H}} (the simple graph in which the vertices are {{mvar|E}} and two elements of {{mvar|E}} are linked if and only if they intersect) is a [[perfect graph]].

== Matching and packing ==
The problem of '''[[set packing]]''' is equivalent to hypergraph matching.

A '''[[vertex packing|vertex-packing]]''' in a (simple) graph is a subset {{mvar|P}} of its vertices, such that no two vertices in {{mvar|P}} are adjacent.

The problem of finding a maximum vertex-packing in a graph is equivalent to the problem of finding a maximum matching in a hypergraph:<ref name="lp" />{{rp|467}}

* Given a hypergraph {{math|1=''H'' = (''V'', ''E'')}},  define its ''intersection graph'' {{math|Int(''H'')}} as the simple graph whose vertices are {{mvar|E}} and whose edges are pairs {{math|(''e''{{sub|1}},''e''{{sub|2}})}} such that {{math|''e''{{sub|1}}}}, {{math|''e''{{sub|2}}}} have a vertex in common.  Then every matching in {{mvar|H}} is a vertex-packing in {{math|Int(''H'')}} and vice versa.
* Given a graph {{math|1=''G'' = (''V' '', ''E' '')}}, define its ''star hypergraph'' {{math|St(''G'')}} as the hypergraph whose vertices are {{mvar|E'}} and whose hyperedges are the [[Star (graph theory)|stars]] of the vertices of {{mvar|G}} (i.e., for each vertex {{mvar|v'}} in {{mvar|V'}}, there is a hyperedge in {{math|St(''G'')}} that contains all edges in {{mvar|E'}} that are adjacent to {{mvar|v'}}).  Then every vertex-packing in {{mvar|G}} is a matching in {{math|St(''G'')}} and vice versa. 
* Alternatively, given a graph {{math|1=''G'' = (''V' '', ''E' '')}}, define its ''clique hypergraph'' {{math|Cl(''G'')}} as the hypergraph whose vertices are the [[Clique (graph theory)|cliques]] of {{mvar|G}},  and for each vertex {{mvar|v'}} in {{mvar|V'}}, there is a hyperedge in {{math|Cl(''G'')}} containing all cliques in {{mvar|G}} that contain {{mvar|v'}}.  Then again, every vertex-packing in {{mvar|G}} is a matching in {{math|Cl(''G'')}} and vice versa. Note that {{math|Cl(''G'')}} cannot be constructed from {{mvar|G}} in [[polynomial time]], so it cannot be used as a reduction for proving NP-hardness. But it has some theoretical uses.
